name: Lead with the why
summary: Open a direction-setting conversation with the purpose behind the work before the what and the how, so people can make their own trade-offs.
how_to_apply: Before assigning work or announcing a change, say in one or two sentences what outcome it serves and why it matters to customers, the business or the team. Then the what, then the how.
example_line: The reason this matters is that clients are leaving at renewal; everything in this plan is about fixing that.
markers: Purpose or outcome statement in Tom's first turns on an item ('the reason', 'so that', 'because')
Task instructions that arrive with no stated reason
Others later restating the purpose in their own words
common_mistakes: Purpose so abstract it gives no guidance ('to be world class')
Giving the why once and never repeating it
Treating why-first as a scientific finding; the brain claims behind it are not supported
drill: For the next five requests Tom makes, start each with 'The reason this matters is...' and keep it under 20 words.

name: Paint a concrete picture of success
summary: Describe what the future looks like when the goal is met, in specific and sensory terms, rather than abstract aims.
how_to_apply: When setting a goal, describe a day or a customer moment in the future state: who is doing what, what has changed, what number moved.
example_line: In a year, a new client should be live in two weeks, not three months, and the onboarding team should be bored.
markers: Future-tense descriptions with concrete nouns, numbers or people
Others asking 'what does good look like?' (absence of picture)
common_mistakes: Hype without specifics
A picture so detailed it dictates the method
drill: Write a three-sentence 'day in the life after we win' for Tom's current top priority and use it to open the next team meeting.

name: One thematic goal for now
summary: Name a single, time-bound rallying priority that everyone on the leadership team shares, on top of their normal jobs.
how_to_apply: Agree one qualitative goal for the next few months, plus a handful of defining objectives, and review progress against it at every leadership meeting.
example_line: For the next quarter our one thing is fixing onboarding; if a request doesn't help that, it waits.
markers: A single named priority referenced across meetings
Agenda items explicitly linked to (or parked against) the priority
Count of 'top priorities' named (more than three is diluted)
common_mistakes: Calling five things the top priority
Setting the goal and then never referring to it
drill: At the start of each leadership meeting this month, state the thematic goal and ask for one red/amber/green on it from each person.

name: Say what we will not do
summary: Make strategy real by naming the things the team will stop or decline, not just the things it will do.
how_to_apply: With every priority, name at least one thing that is deprioritised or stopped, and say who will tell affected stakeholders.
example_line: We're pausing the partner portal until March. That's the trade for getting onboarding fixed.
markers: Explicit 'not', 'stop', 'pause', 'park' choices in direction-setting talk
Trade-off language ('the cost of this is')
common_mistakes: Adding priorities without removing any
Stopping work silently so teams find out late
drill: For each priority Tom sets this week, add one 'and therefore we will not...' sentence.

name: State commander's intent
summary: Give the purpose, the desired end state and the key constraints, so people can act sensibly when the plan meets reality.
how_to_apply: When briefing, cover three things: the purpose, what done looks like, and the limits (budget, risk, deadlines). Leave the method to the team.
example_line: The intent is a signed pilot by end of November; stay inside the existing budget and don't commit us to custom builds.
markers: Purpose + end state + constraints in one briefing turn
Low share of 'how' instructions from Tom
Follow-up questions from the team about goals (fewer is better) vs about method (fine)
common_mistakes: Giving steps but no end state
Constraints so tight they become the method
drill: Before the next delegation, write the intent in three lines (purpose, end state, limits) and read it out.

name: Set specific, stretching goals
summary: Specific, challenging goals tend to beat 'do your best' because they focus effort and allow progress to be measured.
how_to_apply: Turn vague aims into a measurable outcome with a date and a level that is hard but believable; agree how progress will be seen.
example_line: Let's aim for churn under 8 percent by June; we're at 12, so that's a real stretch.
markers: Numbers and dates in goal statements
Vague goals ('improve', 'do better', 'as soon as possible')
common_mistakes: Goals so hard nobody believes them
Specific goals on narrow metrics that invite gaming
Hard goals on complex, novel tasks where learning goals work better
drill: Rewrite each goal Tom states in his next three meetings as 'from X to Y by when'.

name: Technical or adaptive?
summary: Distinguish problems experts can fix from problems that need people to change their habits, values or loyalties, and lead each differently.
how_to_apply: Ask aloud whether a known fix exists. If not, treat it as adaptive: involve the people affected, expect discomfort, and do not hand down a solution.
example_line: There's no playbook for this one; the fix is going to mean sales changing how they qualify deals, so they need to own it.
markers: Problem classification language ('is this a known fix?')
Tom offering a quick technical answer to a people-change problem
common_mistakes: Treating every problem as technical because that's comfortable
Labelling avoidance as 'adaptive' to dodge a decision
drill: Pick the three hardest open issues; for each, Tom states aloud in the meeting whether it is technical or adaptive and why.

name: Get on the balcony
summary: Step back mid-discussion to observe the pattern of the conversation and the system, not just the content.
how_to_apply: When a discussion loops or heats up, pause and describe what is happening ('we keep coming back to X; maybe the real issue is Y'), then ask if others see it.
example_line: Can I step back for a second? We've debated price three times; I think the real disagreement is about which customers we want.
markers: Meta-comments about the discussion itself
Repeated topic loops before a reframe
Reframes followed by a change in discussion direction
common_mistakes: Stepping back so often nothing gets decided
Observations that sound like judgements of people
drill: In each meeting, make one 'balcony' observation about the pattern of the conversation and check it with the group.

name: Confront the brutal facts with faith
summary: Combine plain acknowledgement of the hardest facts with steady confidence that the team will prevail.
how_to_apply: State the worst current facts without softening, then state why you believe the team can still win and what you'll do.
example_line: We lost the two biggest bids this quarter. That's real. I still think we win this market, and here's how.
markers: Unhedged statement of bad facts
Optimism without facts (denial) or facts without a path (despair)
common_mistakes: Sugar-coating bad news to protect morale
Over-dramatising to create urgency
drill: When next reporting bad news, use two sentences: 'The facts are...' and 'What I believe and will do is...'.

name: Label facts, assumptions and judgements
sub_capability: Thinking out loud: assumptions and trade-offs
summary: When explaining a view, say which parts are known, which are assumed and which are judgement, so others can test the weak links.
how_to_apply: Use explicit tags while reasoning aloud: 'the fact is', 'I'm assuming', 'my judgement is'. Ask which assumption others would challenge first.
example_line: Fact: three pilots converted. Assumption: the next ten look like them. That second bit is where I'd push.
markers: Tags such as 'assuming', 'my guess', 'we know' in Tom's reasoning turns
Questions that target assumptions
common_mistakes: Presenting a guess with the certainty of a fact
So many caveats the view is lost
drill: In the next strategy discussion, Tom names his top two assumptions out loud and asks the group to attack them.

name: Speak in probabilities
sub_capability: Thinking out loud: assumptions and trade-offs
summary: Express uncertain judgements as likelihoods rather than certainties, which invites calibration and better debate.
how_to_apply: Replace 'this will work' with a rough percentage and the reason; invite others to give their own number before discussing.
example_line: I'd put it at about 60 percent that the regulator signs off by spring. What would you say?
markers: Numeric likelihoods or 'how sure are you?' questions
Absolute words ('definitely', 'no way') on uncertain matters (see `certainty_per_100w`)
common_mistakes: False precision ('63.5 percent')
Using probabilities to avoid committing to a decision
drill: For one week, every forecast Tom gives in a meeting includes a percentage; review hit rates monthly.

name: Model the reasoning, not just the answer
sub_capability: Thinking out loud: assumptions and trade-offs
summary: Share how you got to a view (criteria, options rejected, what would change your mind), so the team learns to think strategically.
how_to_apply: After giving a conclusion, spend a minute on the path: what you weighed, what you dropped and why, and what evidence would change your mind.
example_line: I landed on B. A was cheaper but locks us in; C needed people we don't have. If the pilot fails, I'd switch to A.
markers: 'What would change my mind' statements
Options rejected with reasons
Long monologues of reasoning (`longest_turn_s`) without a question at the end
common_mistakes: Lecturing
Reasoning aloud so long that others defer instead of challenging
drill: After each decision Tom announces, add one sentence of 'what would change my mind'.

name: Diagnose the situation type
summary: Different business situations (start-up, turnaround, accelerated growth, realignment, sustaining success) call for different priorities and leadership styles.
how_to_apply: In a new role or initiative, name aloud which situation each part of the portfolio is in and what that implies for pace and style.
example_line: The core product is a realignment, people don't yet accept it's in trouble; the new unit is a pure start-up.
markers: Situation labels in early-tenure conversations
Style matched to situation (directive in turnaround, consultative in realignment)
common_mistakes: Applying the playbook from the last job
Treating the whole organisation as one situation
drill: List Tom's three main areas, label each STARS type, and share it with his boss to check agreement.

name: Agree expectations with the boss early
summary: Hold explicit conversations with the boss on the situation, expectations, working style, resources and personal development.
how_to_apply: Plan the topics across early 1:1s with the boss and check alignment on what success looks like and by when.
example_line: Before I go further, can we agree what you'd need to see by March for this to count as a success?
markers: Upward conversations containing explicit expectation-setting questions
Agreement summaries ('so by March you want...')
common_mistakes: Assuming the boss's priorities
Only meeting the boss to report
drill: Book five boss conversations over a month, one per theme, and record a one-line agreement after each.

name: Name who has the D
summary: For each significant decision, make clear who recommends, who must agree, who gives input, who decides and who carries it out.
how_to_apply: When a decision item opens, say who decides and what role everyone else in the room plays. If it isn't clear, settle that first.
example_line: Sam, this is your call; the rest of us are input. Legal has a veto only on the contract terms.
markers: Decider statement at the start of a decision item
Re-opened decisions or 'I thought I was deciding' disputes
Too many people with a veto
common_mistakes: Using the roles as a bureaucratic sign-off chain
Naming a decider and then overruling them in the meeting
drill: For the next three cross-team decisions, write the R, A, P, I and D roles in the meeting note before discussion starts.

name: Say which decision style you're using
summary: Tell people whether you are informing them of a decision, consulting them before you decide, or asking them to decide together, so input isn't mistaken for a vote.
how_to_apply: Before discussion, state the mode: 'I've decided, here's why'; 'I'll decide after hearing you'; or 'we'll decide together'. Stick to it.
example_line: I want your views, but I'll make the call on Friday and tell you why.
markers: Explicit mode statement
Frustration signals afterwards ('I thought we were voting')
common_mistakes: Pretending to consult on a decision already made
Switching from consensus to command mid-meeting without saying so
drill: In every decision item for two weeks, Tom states the mode in his first sentence.

name: Widen beyond whether-or-not
summary: Decisions framed as a single yes/no option tend to fail more often than those weighing several alternatives.
how_to_apply: When a proposal arrives as 'should we do X?', ask for at least one genuine alternative and a 'what if we couldn't do X?' option before judging.
example_line: Before we say yes, what else could we do with the same money?
markers: Number of distinct options named per decision item
Yes/no framings ('should we', 'whether to') with no alternatives
common_mistakes: Adding straw-man options to make the favourite look good
Option overload with no criteria
drill: For each decision this month, Tom asks 'what's option two?' before anyone argues for option one.

name: Agree criteria before preferences
summary: Settle how options will be judged before people state which they prefer, reducing motivated reasoning.
how_to_apply: List two to four criteria and their rough weights, then score the options, then discuss preferences.
example_line: Let's agree what matters first: payback, risk to the core, and team capacity. Then we'll look at options.
markers: Criteria stated before options are debated
Preferences voiced before any criteria
common_mistakes: Criteria chosen after the fact to justify a favourite
Over-engineering small decisions
drill: On the next significant decision, write criteria on the whiteboard before options are discussed.

name: Speak last on contested calls
summary: When the leader states a view first, others tend to anchor on it or fall silent; holding back until others speak surfaces more information.
how_to_apply: On contested items, ask each person for their view before giving your own; say explicitly that you'll share yours last.
example_line: I'll hold my view till the end. Priya, start us off: what would you do?
markers: Order of opinion: Tom's first stance vs others' first stance on the item
Number of distinct speakers before Tom's view
common_mistakes: Signalling a view with tone or leading questions while 'speaking last'
Using it on trivial decisions and slowing everything
drill: In the next five team decisions, the coach checks whether Tom's first opinion comes after at least two others.

name: Collect independent views first
summary: Ask people to form and record their judgement independently before group discussion, so the group gets genuinely separate estimates.
how_to_apply: Before a decision meeting, ask for written views or scores; in the room, have everyone note their answer before anyone speaks.
example_line: Write down your number for next year's revenue before we discuss. Then we'll compare.
markers: Requests for pre-reads, written views or silent scoring
Discussion starting with the most senior person's view
common_mistakes: Collecting views and ignoring the spread
Using it on decisions that need creativity rather than estimation
drill: For the next forecast or estimate, run a silent-write round before discussion and compare spread.

name: Ask for the strongest case against
summary: Explicitly invite the best argument against the favoured option; genuine dissent improves decision quality more than role-played dissent.
how_to_apply: Before converging, ask: 'What's the strongest case against this?' and 'Who disagrees, even partly?' Reward the person who answers.
example_line: We're all nodding. Who's got the best argument for not doing this?
markers: Dissent invitations
Disagreement turns from others after the invitation
Tom's response to dissent: explores vs dismisses
common_mistakes: Assigning a token devil's advocate and treating the exercise as box-ticking
Inviting dissent then arguing it down immediately
drill: In each decision item, Tom asks for the case against at least once and summarises it fairly before deciding.

name: Run a pre-mortem
summary: Imagine the decision has failed and ask everyone to write the reasons why, which surfaces risks people otherwise keep quiet about.
how_to_apply: Before committing, say: 'It's a year from now and this has failed. Take two minutes and write why.' Collect reasons and adjust the plan.
example_line: Let's assume this launch flopped. What went wrong? Two minutes, write it down, then we'll go round.
markers: Pre-mortem framing ('imagine it failed')
Number of distinct risks raised
Plan changes after the exercise
common_mistakes: Running it after the decision is locked
Letting it become general pessimism without actions
drill: Run a ten-minute pre-mortem on the next project before kick-off; the coach checks for at least three new risks and an owner per mitigation.

name: Weigh views by track record
summary: Give more weight to people with relevant track records and clear reasoning, while still hearing everyone.
how_to_apply: When views conflict, ask each person about their experience with this type of decision and their reasoning; weigh accordingly and say so.
example_line: You've run three of these launches; walk me through why you'd wait.
markers: Questions about relevant experience
Explicit weighting statements
common_mistakes: Using 'believability' to dismiss junior or unconventional views
Mistaking seniority for track record
drill: On the next contested call, Tom asks each contributor 'how many times have you seen this play out?' before weighing views.

name: Two-way doors move fast
summary: Separate reversible decisions, which should be made quickly by small groups, from hard-to-reverse ones that deserve a slow, careful process.
how_to_apply: Ask aloud: 'Can we undo this cheaply?' If yes, decide now with roughly 70 percent of the information. If no, slow down and widen input.
example_line: This is reversible; let's pick one today and check in a month.
markers: Reversibility language
Items deferred repeatedly across recordings
Heavy process on small calls
common_mistakes: Calling irreversible things reversible to rush them
Never revisiting the reversible decision
drill: Tag every decision in Tom's meetings this week as one-way or two-way and track time-to-decision.

name: Decide or set the decision date
summary: Avoid open-ended deferral: either decide now or name what information is missing, who gets it, and when the decision will be made.
how_to_apply: If you can't decide in the meeting, say what would make it decidable, assign it, and set the date and decider.
example_line: We can't call this yet. Ali gets the costings by Tuesday; I decide Wednesday.
markers: Deferral statements without date/owner
Same item resurfacing undecided in later recordings
common_mistakes: Asking for more data to avoid discomfort
Setting dates then letting them slip silently
drill: For each deferred item, Tom must say 'missing info, owner, decision date'; the coach flags any deferral without all three.

name: State the decision in one sentence
summary: Close each decision item with a clear sentence of what was decided, so nobody leaves with a different version.
how_to_apply: End the item with 'So we've decided...' plus any key condition, and ask if anyone heard it differently.
example_line: So: we launch in the UK only, in March, at the current price. Anyone hear something different?
markers: Decision sentence at the end of the item
Items ending without a stated outcome
common_mistakes: Summarising so vaguely it can mean anything
Skipping the check that others heard the same
drill: The coach counts decision items with a closing decision sentence; target 100 percent for two weeks.

name: Disagree and commit
summary: After real debate, people who disagreed commit fully to the decision; the leader can model this by committing to calls they argued against.
how_to_apply: Once a decision is made, ask dissenters explicitly whether they can commit, and say you will back it in front of others.
example_line: I'd have gone the other way, but I'll back this fully, and I won't relitigate it.
markers: Explicit commitment checks
Later relitigation of settled decisions across recordings
common_mistakes: Using the phrase to shut down debate before it happens
Demanding commitment from people never actually heard
drill: After each contested decision, Tom asks each dissenter 'can you commit to this?' and notes the answer.
ethics_note: Can be used to silence legitimate concerns or rush debate; only valid after dissent was genuinely heard.

name: Judge the decision, not the outcome
summary: A bad outcome does not prove a bad decision; review the information, process and judgement separately from luck.
how_to_apply: In reviews, ask what was knowable at the time, whether the process was sound, and what part was luck, before assigning credit or blame.
example_line: It went badly, but given what we knew in June, was the call itself wrong?
markers: 'Resulting' language ('it failed, so it was a mistake')
Separate discussion of process and outcome in reviews
common_mistakes: Using 'bad luck' to excuse poor process
Never revisiting decisions that went well by luck
drill: In the next post-mortem, Tom splits the discussion into 'what we knew', 'how we decided', 'what was luck'.

name: Keep a decision journal
summary: Record major decisions with the reasoning, expected outcome and confidence at the time, to learn honestly later.
how_to_apply: For significant calls, note in two minutes: the decision, options, expected result, confidence, and what would make it wrong. Review quarterly.
example_line: Let's log this: we expect 20 sign-ups by June, I'm 60 percent on it, and we'll look again in July.
markers: Spoken logging of expected outcomes and confidence
Later references to the logged expectation
common_mistakes: Writing it after the fact
Logging but never reviewing
drill: Start a decision log; Tom adds one entry per week and reviews the first batch in three months.

name: Who does what by when
summary: Every agreed action gets one named owner, a concrete deliverable and a date, spoken aloud and confirmed.
how_to_apply: When an action comes up, stop and pin it: name, verb, deliverable, date. Ask the owner to confirm out loud.
example_line: So Dan, you'll send the revised pricing to the client by Thursday noon. That work?
markers: Name + verb + date triplets in Tom's turns
Owner's verbal acceptance in the next turn
Actions phrased with 'we' or 'someone' as owner
common_mistakes: 'We should look at that' with no owner
Two owners for one action
Dates like 'soon' or 'next week-ish'
drill: The coach counts actions in Tom's meetings and flags any without owner and date; target is zero gaps for a fortnight.

name: Turn intentions into if-then plans
summary: Commitments stated as 'when X happens, I will do Y' are more likely to be carried out than general intentions.
how_to_apply: When someone commits, help them name the trigger and the first step: when and where they'll start, and what they'll do if blocked.
example_line: When the numbers land on Monday, what's the first thing you'll do with them?
markers: Follow-up questions on when/where the first step happens
Commitments with a concrete trigger
common_mistakes: Turning every action into a detailed plan
Doing the planning for the person
drill: In 1:1s this month, for each new commitment Tom asks 'when exactly will you start, and what's step one?'.

name: Get the owner to say it back
summary: Ask the owner to restate the action in their own words; misunderstandings surface before work starts.
how_to_apply: After assigning, ask: 'Can you play back what you're taking away?' Correct any gaps there and then.
example_line: Before we move on, can you tell me what you're doing and by when, just so I know I've been clear?
markers: Playback requests
Owner restatements that differ from Tom's version
common_mistakes: Making it sound like a test of the person rather than of Tom's clarity
drill: In the next five delegations, Tom asks for a playback and notes any mismatch.

name: Open with last time's actions
summary: Start recurring meetings by reviewing the commitments from the previous one, owner by owner, briefly and without drama.
how_to_apply: First five minutes: read the action list, ask each owner done / not done / new date. Explore misses after the review, not during.
example_line: Quick run through last week's actions. Dan, pricing to the client: done?
markers: References to previous actions in the first minutes
Actions from one recording reappearing (or vanishing) in the next
common_mistakes: Turning the review into a status monologue
Shaming people for misses in front of the group
drill: For a month, every meeting Tom chairs starts with the previous action list; the coach checks the first five minutes.

name: Make progress visible against goals
summary: Regularly review progress on a small set of goals with the team, so people can see where they stand.
how_to_apply: Pick the two or three measures that matter, review them in the same order every week, and ask what the trend means for actions.
example_line: Same three numbers as always. Onboarding time is flat for three weeks: what's stuck?
markers: Standing metrics reviewed across recordings
Discussion moving from number to action
common_mistakes: Too many metrics to discuss
Reviewing numbers without deciding anything
drill: Choose three team measures; Tom reviews them first in each weekly meeting for six weeks.

name: Own it first
summary: When something goes wrong in Tom's area, he takes responsibility publicly before discussing others' parts.
how_to_apply: Open failure discussions with what Tom could have done differently (briefing, resourcing, follow-up), then move to fixes.
example_line: That slipped because I didn't make the priority clear. Let's fix that first.
markers: First-person ownership statements ('that's on me', 'I should have')
Blame or excuse phrases ('they didn't', 'if only')
common_mistakes: Performative self-blame that blocks real analysis
Owning everything so others never learn to own theirs
drill: In each review of a miss, Tom's first statement names one thing he'll do differently; the coach checks the first Tom turn.

name: No bad teams, check the briefing
summary: Treat a team's poor performance first as a question about the leader's clarity, priorities and support.
how_to_apply: Before criticising execution, ask the team: 'What wasn't clear from me? What did you need that you didn't get?'
example_line: Before we look at what went wrong on your side, what did I leave unclear?
markers: Questions about leader clarity and support in reviews
common_mistakes: Using it rhetorically and then blaming anyway
drill: After the next missed deadline, Tom asks his team two questions about his own briefing before anything else.
