name: Name the gap, then ask
summary: When a commitment is missed, describe the expected and actual result factually, then ask what happened before judging.
how_to_apply: State: 'We agreed X by Tuesday; it's not done.' Then ask an open question and listen. Diagnose whether it's motivation or ability, then agree the fix.
example_line: We agreed the deck by Tuesday and it isn't in. What got in the way?
markers: Expected vs actual statement
Open question immediately after
Avoidance: misses not mentioned at all
common_mistakes: Sarcasm or sighing
Rescuing by doing it himself
Lecturing before asking
drill: The next time a commitment is missed, Tom uses the gap-then-question pattern within the same meeting; the coach checks the wording.

name: Diagnose motivation vs ability
summary: Work out whether a miss is about willingness or capability (or the system), because each needs a different response.
how_to_apply: Ask about obstacles and skills before assuming lack of effort: 'Is this about time, know-how, or something else?'
example_line: Is this a time problem, a know-how problem, or something about how the work's set up?
markers: Diagnostic questions separating skill, will and system
Assumptions of laziness voiced without inquiry
common_mistakes: Jumping to motivation lectures
Ignoring structural causes (Tom's own priorities)
drill: In each accountability conversation, Tom asks one question about ability and one about obstacles before suggesting a fix.

name: Agree the consequence and check-in
summary: End accountability conversations with an explicit plan, a check-in date and, where needed, what happens if it slips again.
how_to_apply: Close with: new commitment, how Tom will check, and the consequence if missed, stated calmly.
example_line: New date is Friday; I'll check in Thursday. If it slips again, I'll need to move it to someone else.
markers: New date + check-in + consequence in the close
Open-ended endings ('let's try harder')
common_mistakes: Threats delivered in anger
Consequences never enforced
drill: For the next three accountability conversations, the coach checks the last minute for date, check-in and consequence.

name: Peer accountability in the room
summary: Encourage team members to hold each other to commitments rather than routing everything through the leader.
how_to_apply: When one team member's miss affects another, invite the affected peer to say so directly in the meeting, and model doing it respectfully.
example_line: Sara, this delay hits your launch. What do you need from Dan?
markers: Peer-to-peer challenges in meetings
All accountability flowing through Tom
common_mistakes: Pitting people against each other
Abdicating to peers when Tom's intervention is needed
drill: In the next team meeting, Tom hands at least one cross-team dependency to the two peers to resolve in the room.

name: Run a quick after-action review
summary: After a milestone or setback, ask what was meant to happen, what happened, why, and what to do differently; structured debriefs reliably improve performance.
how_to_apply: Run the four questions within days of the event, keep it to 15-30 minutes, focus on process not blame, and end with one or two changes with owners.
example_line: Four questions: what did we expect, what happened, why the gap, and what do we change next time?
markers: Debrief structure in the transcript
Blame language vs process language
Actions coming out of the review
common_mistakes: Debriefing only failures
Turning it into a blame session
Lists of lessons with no owner
drill: After the next milestone, Tom runs a 20-minute after-action review; the coach checks the four questions and a closing action.

name: Blameless curiosity about mistakes
summary: Separate blameworthy acts from honest errors and complex-system failures, and respond to the latter with curiosity.
how_to_apply: Ask 'what made that seem like the right move at the time?' and 'what in the system made this easy to get wrong?'
example_line: What made that look like the right call at the time? I'm asking to fix the process, not to blame.
markers: System-focused questions
Blame language ('who did this')
common_mistakes: Blamelessness applied to genuine negligence
Saying 'no blame' then blaming
drill: In the next incident review, Tom asks at least two system questions before any question about individual decisions.

name: From 'can I' to 'I intend to'
summary: Shift reports from asking permission to stating what they intend to do, so they do the thinking and the leader only approves or questions.
how_to_apply: When asked 'should I...?' or 'can I...?', reply 'tell me what you intend to do'. Over time, ask them to come with intentions, not questions.
example_line: Don't ask me; tell me what you intend to do and why.
markers: Reports' phrasing over time: 'can I / what should I' vs 'I intend to / I plan to'
Tom's replies to permission requests
common_mistakes: Using it with people new to the task who need guidance
Rubber-stamping without engaging with the reasoning
drill: For a month, whenever a report asks permission, Tom replies with 'what do you intend to do?'; the coach tracks the shift in reports' language.

name: Delegate the decision, not just the task
summary: Hand over authority for the outcome along with the work, with clear limits, rather than retaining every call.
how_to_apply: Say explicitly which decisions the person owns and which still need Tom, and resist taking them back.
example_line: You own the vendor choice; just bring me in if it goes over 50k.
markers: Statements of decision authority in delegation
Tom later reopening the delegated call
common_mistakes: Delegating the work and keeping the decisions
Dumping without limits or support
drill: In each delegation this week, Tom states 'you decide X; I decide Y'.

name: Use the ladder of involvement
summary: Make the level of delegation explicit: from 'tell me what's happening' through 'recommend', 'decide and tell me', to 'decide, no need to tell me'.
how_to_apply: When handing something over, say which level applies and when it will move up.
example_line: On this one, decide and tell me afterwards. After the first two, you won't need to tell me.
markers: Explicit delegation level stated
Mismatch: Tom asking for updates on things he's handed over fully
common_mistakes: Leaving the level unsaid
Moving people down the ladder after one mistake without saying so
drill: Tom labels each delegated item with a level for two weeks; reports confirm they heard it.

name: Adjust to task-relevant maturity
summary: The right amount of direction depends on how experienced the person is with this particular task, not their seniority overall.
how_to_apply: Before delegating, ask the person how often they've done this; give structure for novices and space for experts, and say what you're doing.
example_line: You've not done a board paper before, so let's agree the outline together and then I'll get out of the way.
markers: Questions about experience with the task
Instruction detail relative to stated experience
common_mistakes: Micromanaging experts
Abandoning novices
Treating situational models as proven; research support is weak
drill: Before each delegation, Tom asks one experience question and states how closely he'll be involved.

name: Agree the check-in rhythm up front
summary: Set how and when progress will be checked at the start, so follow-up feels planned rather than intrusive.
how_to_apply: When delegating, agree the first check-in date and what you want to see, and drop ad hoc 'any update?' requests.
example_line: Let's look at a first draft Wednesday; until then it's yours.
markers: Check-in plan in delegation turns
Unplanned 'any news?' questions on delegated work
common_mistakes: Check-ins so frequent they become control
drill: Every delegation Tom makes for two weeks includes a named first check-in.

name: Don't take the monkey
summary: When someone brings a problem, help them own the next step instead of taking the problem away.
how_to_apply: Ask 'what do you think we should do?' and 'what's your next step?' before offering to act. End with the action sitting with them.
example_line: Good catch. What do you think the options are, and which would you go for?
markers: Tom's turn after a problem statement: question vs offer to do it
Count of actions Tom takes at the close vs others
common_mistakes: Refusing to help when the person is genuinely stuck
Asking 'what do you think?' with a fixed answer in mind
drill: The coach counts actions Tom volunteers to take in 1:1s; aim to halve them over a month.

name: Ask before you answer
summary: Leaders who answer every question train teams to stop thinking; asking first develops judgement and surfaces better ideas.
how_to_apply: When asked for an answer, ask one question first ('what are you leaning towards?'). Answer only if they're stuck or it's urgent.
example_line: What would you do if I weren't here?
markers: Question-before-answer pattern in Tom's turns
Ask:tell ratio in response to team questions
common_mistakes: Socratic questioning in a crisis
Making people guess what Tom wants
drill: For one week, Tom's first response to every 'what should I do' is a question; the coach checks.

name: Explain the why and offer choice
summary: Leaders who give rationale, offer choices and acknowledge others' views tend to have more motivated and better-performing people.
how_to_apply: When asking for something, give the reason, offer a choice where possible (how, when, which first), and acknowledge any constraint the person faces.
example_line: I need this by Friday because of the board. Would you rather drop the market sizing or push the competitor piece?
markers: Rationale statements
Choice offers
Controlling language ('you must', 'just do it')
common_mistakes: Fake choices
Long justifications for trivial requests
drill: In 1:1s for two weeks, every request Tom makes includes a reason and, where possible, a choice.

name: Acknowledge their perspective before directing
summary: Show you understand the other person's view or constraint before asking them to do something different.
how_to_apply: Briefly reflect their position ('I know this lands on top of the audit'), then make the ask.
example_line: I know you're stretched with the audit; this still has to come first, and here's why.
markers: Perspective acknowledgement before directives
common_mistakes: Acknowledgement as a formula followed by ignoring it
drill: Tom precedes his next five directive requests with one sentence acknowledging the person's situation.

name: Offer a stretch with backing
summary: Give people challenges a little beyond what they've done, make the stretch explicit and say why you think they can do it.
how_to_apply: Name the stretch, the reason you chose them, and the support available; let them present the outcome themselves.
example_line: This is bigger than anything you've run, and that's the point. I think you're ready, and I'll be your sounding board.
markers: Stretch framing + confidence statement
Others presenting their own work in meetings vs Tom presenting it
common_mistakes: Stretch without support
Taking back the visible part (the presentation) at the end
drill: Over a month, the coach counts how often reports present their own work in Tom's meetings vs Tom presenting it.

name: Ask for the big question, not the answer
summary: Frame a challenge as a question or opportunity the team must work out, rather than handing down a solution.
how_to_apply: Describe the challenge and why it matters, ask the team how they'd tackle it, and let them fill the gap.
example_line: How could we halve onboarding time without new headcount? I don't know yet; that's what I want from you.
markers: Challenges posed as open questions
Tom supplying the answer within the same turn
common_mistakes: Asking a question you've already answered
Challenges that are impossible
drill: Next planning session: Tom frames one challenge purely as a question and doesn't offer an answer for 15 minutes.

name: Start with 'what's on your mind?'
summary: Open coaching conversations with a broad, focused question that lets the other person choose what matters most.
how_to_apply: Begin 1:1s with an open question about their priorities, then let them lead; don't start with your own list.
example_line: What's on your mind this week?
markers: Who raises the first topic in a 1:1
Tom's opening question type
common_mistakes: Asking then immediately jumping to Tom's own agenda
drill: In every 1:1 for a month, Tom's first question is open and he lets the report choose the topic.

name: And what else?
summary: The first answer is rarely the whole story; a simple follow-up prompt draws out more options and the real issue.
how_to_apply: After someone answers, ask 'and what else?' two or three times before moving on.
example_line: And what else is going on with that?
markers: Repeated follow-up prompts
Length of the other person's answers after prompts
common_mistakes: Using it mechanically so it sounds scripted
Asking it once and stopping
drill: In the next three 1:1s, Tom uses 'and what else?' at least twice; the coach checks for new content afterwards.

name: Find the real challenge
summary: Help people focus on the core issue for them, rather than solving the first problem they mention.
how_to_apply: Ask 'what's the real challenge here for you?' and stay with the person's own part of it.
example_line: Of all that, what's the real challenge for you?
markers: Focusing questions after a broad description
Tom solving the first problem raised
common_mistakes: Pushing for the 'real' issue when the surface one is real
drill: Use the focus question in each coaching conversation this week before giving any input.

name: Ask more, follow up more
summary: People who ask more questions, especially follow-ups, are liked more and learn more; leaders underestimate this.
how_to_apply: Aim for most of Tom's turns in a 1:1 to be questions, and make most of those build on what the person just said.
example_line: You said the client went quiet after the demo; what changed in that meeting?
markers: Tom's `questions` per turn
Follow-ups that reference the prior turn
Report `talk_share` in 1:1s
common_mistakes: Questions that are disguised advice
Interrogation without warmth
drill: The coach reports Tom's question share and follow-up count after each 1:1; aim for at least half of his turns as questions.

name: Stay curious a little longer
summary: Delay giving advice; the urge to fix often leads to solving the wrong problem and undercuts the other person's thinking.
how_to_apply: Before offering a view, ask at least three questions. When you do advise, say it's one option and ask what they think.
example_line: I've got a thought, but first: what have you already tried?
markers: Turns before Tom's first recommendation
Leading questions ('have you thought about...?') counted as advice
common_mistakes: Withholding a crucial answer for the sake of the method
Questions that feel like a trap
drill: In 1:1s, the coach measures how long until Tom's first piece of advice; aim to double it.

name: Don't add too much value
summary: Leaders tend to add their tweak to others' ideas, which lowers the person's ownership more than it improves the idea.
how_to_apply: When someone brings a decent idea, say 'go for it' or ask one question, rather than adding improvements.
example_line: That's good. Run with it.
markers: Tom adding 'one small thing' to others' proposals
'Yes, but' or 'great, and also' patterns
common_mistakes: Letting real flaws go unmentioned
drill: For a week, Tom notes each time he adds to an idea; the coach flags 'great, but' turns.

name: Their meeting, not yours
summary: Regular 1:1s should be driven by the report's agenda, with the manager listening most of the time.
how_to_apply: Ask the report to bring topics; let them talk most of the time; hold Tom's items until the end.
example_line: This is your time. What do you want to cover? I've one thing for the end.
markers: Report `talk_share` in 1:1s (heuristic: above 0.6)
Who raises topics
Tom's `longest_turn_s` in 1:1s
common_mistakes: Cancelling 1:1s when busy
Using them for status updates only
drill: The coach reports Tom's talk share for every 1:1; aim below 0.4.

name: Ask what's getting in the way
summary: Regularly ask about obstacles and whether the manager is part of the problem, then remove blockers.
how_to_apply: In each 1:1, ask 'what's slowing you down?' and 'is there anything I'm doing that makes it harder?'.
example_line: What's slowing you down at the moment, and is any of it me?
markers: Blocker questions
Tom committing to remove a blocker, then reporting back in a later 1:1
common_mistakes: Asking and never acting
drill: Add the blocker question to every 1:1 for a month; the coach checks follow-through in the next 1:1.

sources.where: lazy question: how can I help?

name: Check in on the person, not just the work
summary: Start or end 1:1s with genuine interest in how the person is doing; trust and engagement depend on it.
how_to_apply: Ask a real personal question and listen to the answer before work topics.
example_line: Before we start, how are you doing, honestly?
markers: Personal check-in present
Follow-up on personal matters mentioned before
common_mistakes: Formulaic 'how are you' without waiting for an answer
Prying
drill: Tom opens each 1:1 with a personal question and follows up on what he heard last time.

name: Career conversation in three parts
summary: Understand someone's life story and values, their dreams, and the skills they need next, then link current work to that path.
how_to_apply: Hold a dedicated conversation: what's shaped you, where do you want to be, what do you need to learn. Refer back to it in later 1:1s.
example_line: If this went brilliantly, what would you be doing in five years?
markers: Future-focused questions
References to the person's stated goals in later 1:1s
common_mistakes: Treating it as a one-off HR exercise
Promising promotions
drill: Hold one career conversation with each direct report this quarter; the coach checks later 1:1s for references to their goals.

name: Ask what was most useful
summary: End coaching conversations by asking what the person found most useful, which reinforces learning and gives feedback to the coach.
how_to_apply: Close with: 'What was most useful about this?' and listen.
example_line: What was most useful from this chat?
markers: Learning question in the last minutes
common_mistakes: Fishing for compliments
drill: End every 1:1 for two weeks with the learning question.

name: Teach the thinking behind the call
summary: Develop people's judgement by explaining how you reached a decision, then giving them the next similar one.
how_to_apply: After explaining a call, say 'next time this comes up, you make it, and run it past me'.
example_line: Here's how I weighed it. Next one like this is yours; just run your thinking past me.
markers: Reasoning explanations followed by hand-over statements
common_mistakes: Explaining without ever handing over
drill: After each decision that a report could learn from, Tom adds one hand-over sentence.

name: Coaching style when people want to grow
summary: Coaching works when the person is open to developing; with someone resistant or in a crisis, other styles fit better.
how_to_apply: Before coaching, check the person wants to work on this; if not, switch to direct feedback or direction and say so.
example_line: Is this something you want to work on, or would it help more if I just told you what I'd do?
markers: Readiness or permission questions before coaching
Coaching questions used in a crisis
common_mistakes: Coaching someone who just needs an answer
drill: Before starting a coaching conversation, Tom asks one readiness question.

name: Praise the behaviour and its effect
summary: Specific recognition of what someone did and the difference it made is more useful and believable than generic praise.
how_to_apply: Name the action, the result, and why it mattered, soon after it happens.
example_line: The way you reframed the pricing for the CFO got us the yes. That was the turning point.
markers: Praise statements containing a behaviour and an effect
Generic praise ('great job', 'nice one') with no content
common_mistakes: Praise so frequent it loses meaning
Praise only in private, criticism only in public
drill: In each team meeting, Tom gives one specific piece of praise naming behaviour and effect.

name: Situation, behaviour, impact
summary: Describe the situation, the observable behaviour and its impact, rather than judging the person's character.
how_to_apply: Use three short parts: when and where, what they did (camera view), and what effect it had. Then ask for their view.
example_line: In this morning's client call, you cut in on the CFO twice, and she stopped engaging. How did it feel from your side?
markers: Behaviour descriptions vs trait labels ('you're too...')
Impact stated
Question following the feedback
common_mistakes: Interpretation dressed up as behaviour
Skipping the impact
No space for response
drill: For the next three pieces of critical feedback, the coach checks for situation, behaviour, impact and a question.

name: Care personally, challenge directly
summary: Good feedback shows care for the person and is direct about the problem; avoiding the challenge out of niceness lets people fail.
how_to_apply: Say the hard thing plainly and briefly, and make the care visible (why you're telling them, offer of help).
example_line: I'm telling you because I want you to get the promotion: the board paper wasn't ready.
markers: Direct statement of the issue
Hedge spike on feedback turns (`hedges_per_100w`)
Feedback point never actually stated
common_mistakes: Ruinous empathy: so soft the message is lost
Obnoxious aggression: harsh without care
drill: Before each difficult feedback conversation, Tom writes the one-sentence message and the coach checks it was said within the first two minutes.

name: Skip the feedback sandwich
summary: Wrapping criticism between praise tends to bury the message and make future praise suspect.
how_to_apply: Keep praise and criticism separate; state the criticism clearly on its own and check it landed.
example_line: One thing I want to flag directly, then I want to hear you.
markers: Praise-criticism-praise pattern within one turn
Feedback recipient's playback missing the critical point
common_mistakes: Overcorrecting into criticism with no warmth
drill: The coach flags sandwich patterns in Tom's feedback turns for a month.

name: Keep feedback on the task, not the self
summary: Feedback that draws attention to the person's self-image rather than the task often lowers performance.
how_to_apply: Focus on the work, the gap and how to close it; avoid comments about personality or comparisons with others.
example_line: The analysis is solid; the summary needs to lead with the recommendation.
markers: Task language vs person language ('you are', 'you always')
Comparisons with colleagues
common_mistakes: Vague task comments that give no direction
drill: Review three recent feedback moments with the coach and rewrite any person-focused lines as task-focused.

name: Ask for criticism and embrace the discomfort
summary: Leaders who ask for criticism first make candour safer for everyone; the ask must be specific and the silence tolerated.
how_to_apply: Ask a specific question ('what's one thing I could do differently in these meetings?'), then wait at least six seconds, then thank and act.
example_line: What's one thing I do in these meetings that makes your job harder?
markers: Feedback requests by Tom
Silence length after the request (`median_response_gap_s` around it)
Tom's response to criticism: thanks/questions vs defending
common_mistakes: 'Any feedback?' asked generically
Defending or explaining after receiving it
Asking and never acting
drill: Once a week, Tom asks one specific feedback question in a 1:1 and counts to six before speaking.

name: Thank, don't defend
summary: When receiving criticism, the leader's reaction teaches the team whether candour is safe.
how_to_apply: Respond with thanks and a clarifying question; hold any explanation for later; say what you'll do.
example_line: Thank you, that's useful. Can you give me an example from last week?
markers: Tom's next turn after criticism: thanks/clarifier vs 'yes but', justification
The critic speaking again later in the meeting
common_mistakes: Arguing the point
Over-apologising so the person comforts Tom
drill: The coach flags every 'yes, but' in Tom's response to criticism for a month.

name: Ask for feedforward
summary: Ask for suggestions for the future rather than critiques of the past, which people find easier to give and receive.
how_to_apply: Ask: 'What are two things I could do next month to be better at X?' Listen, thank, don't argue.
example_line: Give me two ideas for how I could run these reviews better next month.
markers: Future-focused feedback requests
common_mistakes: Using feedforward to avoid hearing about real past problems
drill: Tom asks three colleagues for feedforward on one behaviour this month.

name: Two-minute feedback right after
summary: Short, immediate feedback after a meeting or moment is more useful than saving it up for formal reviews.
how_to_apply: Within a day of seeing something worth comment, give a one- or two-minute piece of feedback in private.
example_line: Got two minutes? Quick thought on the client call just now.
markers: Feedback referencing very recent events
Long gaps between event and feedback across recordings
common_mistakes: Saving everything for appraisal
Giving criticism in front of others
drill: Tom gives two impromptu feedback moments a week; the coach checks they reference the same or previous day.

name: Wise feedback: high bar plus belief
summary: Critical feedback is more likely to be accepted and acted on when it states high standards and confidence the person can meet them.
how_to_apply: Before or after critical comments, say plainly that the bar is high and you believe they can reach it.
example_line: I'm being tough on this because it's going to the board and I know you can get it there.
markers: Standards + assurance statements around critique
common_mistakes: Formulaic use without genuine belief
Standards stated but no specific guidance
drill: Add a standards-and-belief line to every substantive piece of critical feedback for a month.

name: Say the uncomfortable thing early
summary: Unclear or delayed feedback is unkind; clarity early saves bigger problems later.
how_to_apply: Raise concerns at the first clear sign, briefly, rather than letting them build up.
example_line: I want to say this now rather than at review time: the timeline's slipping and I'm worried.
markers: Concerns raised at first occurrence vs accumulated
Feedback referring to many past incidents at once (kitchen-sinking)
common_mistakes: Nit-picking every small thing
drill: When Tom notices a concern, he raises it within the same week; the coach flags any feedback that lists three or more old examples.

name: Give credit publicly, by name
summary: Recognising individuals by name in front of peers reinforces the behaviour and signals what the leader values.
how_to_apply: In group settings, credit the specific person and what they did; avoid absorbing credit into 'we' or 'I'.
example_line: This came together because Mo spotted the data issue on Friday.
markers: Credit statements naming people
Tom taking 'I' credit for team work
common_mistakes: Crediting only the visible few
drill: In each team or stakeholder meeting, Tom names one person's contribution specifically.

name: Ask what's behind the position
summary: Positions are what people say they want; interests are why. Agreements are easier when built on interests.
how_to_apply: When someone takes a firm stance, ask 'what's driving that?' or 'what would that give you?', and note shared and different interests.
example_line: Help me understand what the fixed date protects for you.
markers: Interest questions ('why is that important', 'what would that give you')
Repetition of positions by both sides
common_mistakes: Interrogating rather than inquiring
Assuming you know their interest
drill: In the next negotiation or stakeholder disagreement, Tom asks two interest questions before stating his own position.

name: Invent options for mutual gain
summary: Generate several options together before judging any, especially ones that trade on differences in priorities.
how_to_apply: Suggest a short brainstorm with no commitments, then look for trades where each side gets what it values most.
example_line: Let's throw out options without committing. What if you get the date and we get the scope cut?
markers: Option generation language
Trades of low-cost for high-value concessions
common_mistakes: Splitting the difference too early
Brainstorming with no follow-up evaluation
drill: In the next negotiation, Tom proposes at least three package options before settling.

name: Know your walk-away
summary: Being clear on your best alternative if no deal is struck protects against accepting a bad agreement or rejecting a good one.
how_to_apply: Before a negotiation, state aloud (in prep) your best alternative; in the room, compare offers to it rather than to your opening hope.
example_line: If they won't move on exclusivity, our fallback is the second vendor; this has to beat that.
markers: Prep conversations mentioning alternatives
Concessions made with no reference to the alternative
common_mistakes: Revealing a weak alternative
No alternative developed at all
drill: Before each significant negotiation, Tom states his walk-away in a prep call with a colleague.

name: Use objective criteria
summary: Settle disagreements on fair standards (market data, precedent, expert view) rather than will.
how_to_apply: Ask 'what standard would be fair here?' and propose one; agree the standard before the number.
example_line: What's a fair benchmark? Shall we use what others pay for similar contracts?
markers: Appeals to standards, benchmarks, precedent
common_mistakes: Cherry-picking a standard that favours you
drill: In the next pricing or resourcing discussion, Tom proposes an external benchmark before giving a figure.

name: Ask how and what questions
summary: Open questions starting with 'how' or 'what' invite the other side to solve the problem with you and reveal constraints.
how_to_apply: Replace demands with questions like 'how would we make that work?' or 'what's the biggest obstacle on your side?'.
example_line: How am I supposed to make that work with the budget we've got?
markers: 'How'/'what' questions in negotiation turns
'Why' questions that sound accusatory
common_mistakes: Rapid-fire questions that feel like an interrogation
Using them to avoid stating your own needs
drill: In the next stakeholder negotiation, Tom replaces two demands with how/what questions.

name: Label the other side's concern
summary: Naming the emotion or concern you hear ('it sounds like...') can calm a tense exchange and show understanding.
how_to_apply: When you sense resistance, name it neutrally, then pause and let them respond.
example_line: It sounds like you're worried this lands on your team without extra resource.
markers: Labels ('it sounds like', 'it seems like')
Other party's next turn longer and calmer
common_mistakes: Labelling inaccurately or sarcastically
Using labels as a script to manipulate rather than understand
drill: Use one label per tense conversation for two weeks; the coach checks the next turn for de-escalation.
ethics_note: Can slide into manipulation if used to extract concessions rather than to understand; keep it sincere.

name: Anticipate their objections aloud
summary: Naming the other side's likely objections first can lower defensiveness and make it easier to discuss them.
how_to_apply: Before your ask, list the concerns they may have ('you may think this is too late, too expensive...') and invite correction.
example_line: You probably think we're asking too much, too late. That's fair; let me explain why I'm asking anyway.
markers: Pre-emptive acknowledgement of objections
common_mistakes: Exaggerated self-criticism as a tactic
Listing objections they never had
drill: Before the next difficult ask, Tom opens by naming two likely objections.
ethics_note: Used theatrically it can be manipulative; use only to surface real concerns honestly.

name: Pre-wire before the big meeting
summary: Talk to key stakeholders one-to-one before a group decision so surprises and objections surface early.
how_to_apply: In 1:1 soundings, share the draft recommendation, ask for concerns, and adjust; don't ask them to commit secretly.
example_line: Before Thursday I wanted to run this past you: what would stop you supporting it?
markers: Recorded 1:1 soundings before a decision meeting
Questions about concerns and conditions for support
common_mistakes: Backroom deals that make the meeting theatre
Only sounding out allies
drill: Before the next contentious proposal, Tom holds three pre-wire conversations including one likely opponent.

sources.where: find partners, keep the opposition close

ethics_note: Pre-wiring should inform, not bypass, the group decision; avoid secret commitments that hollow out debate.

name: Keep the opposition close
summary: Spend time with those most opposed, understand their losses, and acknowledge them, rather than only courting allies.
how_to_apply: Ask opponents what they stand to lose; acknowledge it explicitly; look for what could reduce it.
example_line: I realise this takes headcount from your area. What would make that less painful?
markers: Conversations with opponents
Acknowledgement of losses
common_mistakes: Ignoring or sidelining opponents
Promising what can't be delivered
drill: Identify the most opposed stakeholder on Tom's top initiative and hold a listening conversation.

sources.where: keep the opposition close, acknowledge loss

name: Bring a recommendation, not just a problem
summary: When raising issues upward, bring options and a recommended course so the boss can decide quickly.
how_to_apply: Structure upward asks: issue, options, recommendation, what you need from them.
example_line: Problem's the supplier delay. Options are wait or switch; I recommend switching. I need your OK on the cost.
markers: Recommendation and explicit ask in upward meetings
Problems raised with no proposal
common_mistakes: Hiding problems until there's a solution
Recommendation buried at the end
drill: For every upward meeting this month, Tom's first two minutes contain the ask and his recommendation.

name: No surprises: flag early
summary: Tell the boss or stakeholders about likely problems early, before they hear it elsewhere.
how_to_apply: Raise risks while they're still risks, with your current view of likelihood and what you're doing.
example_line: Heads-up: there's a 30 percent chance we miss the date. Here's what I'm doing about it.
markers: Early risk flagging with likelihood
Stakeholders reacting to news they heard elsewhere
common_mistakes: Crying wolf on minor risks
Flagging without a plan
drill: Each week Tom names one risk to his boss or key stakeholder with a likelihood and a plan.

name: Frame it in their goals
summary: People are more persuaded by arguments tied to what they care about than by the persuader's reasons.
how_to_apply: Open with their priority, show how the proposal serves it, then give evidence and a concrete example.
example_line: You've said retention is your number one. This proposal is mostly a retention play; here's the evidence.
markers: Audience-centred language ('for you', 'your target')
Proposals framed only in Tom's own terms
common_mistakes: Flattering reframes that misrepresent the proposal
drill: Before the next pitch to a stakeholder, Tom writes their top goal and opens with it.

name: Use consistency with their stated commitments
summary: People prefer to act in line with commitments they've made; linking a request to their stated values or past decisions is persuasive.
how_to_apply: Refer back to what the stakeholder has already said or committed to, and show how the ask follows from it.
example_line: In March you said customer experience comes before margin. This is that choice.
markers: References to the other person's earlier statements or commitments
common_mistakes: Twisting their words
Trapping people with small commitments to extract big ones
drill: In the next influence attempt, Tom links his ask to one thing the stakeholder said previously.
ethics_note: Consistency pressure can become manipulative (foot-in-the-door traps); use only honest, relevant prior commitments.

name: Give first, ask later
summary: Helping others without being asked builds goodwill and a genuine basis for later requests.
how_to_apply: Offer specific help to peers' priorities in conversation; when asking later, the relationship carries it.
example_line: What's your biggest headache this quarter? I might be able to lend you an analyst for it.
markers: Offers of help in peer conversations
Asks made without any prior relationship
common_mistakes: Keeping score out loud
Help with strings openly attached
drill: Tom makes one unprompted offer of help to a peer or stakeholder each week.

name: Ask for advice, not just support
summary: Asking a stakeholder for advice tends to increase how competent they think you are and draws them into the solution.
how_to_apply: Ask a senior stakeholder for their advice on a specific part of the plan, then show you used it.
example_line: You've done three of these integrations. What would you watch out for in ours?
markers: Specific advice requests
Later references to having used the advice
common_mistakes: Asking advice on trivial or obvious matters
Asking and then ignoring it
drill: For the next initiative, Tom asks two stakeholders for specific advice and reports back what he did with it.

name: Mine for hidden disagreement
summary: Teams avoid conflict to stay comfortable; the leader's job is to bring buried disagreement into the open.
how_to_apply: When agreement seems too easy, say so and ask who sees it differently; give permission for the conflict once it starts.
example_line: This was too easy. Who's not convinced? It's fine to push back here.
markers: Dissent invitations
Disagreement turns after invitations
Long silent agreement on major items
common_mistakes: Forcing artificial conflict
Inviting conflict then cutting it off
drill: Once per team meeting, Tom names a moment of possibly false harmony and asks for the dissenting view.

name: Give permission in the moment
summary: When people start to disagree productively, say explicitly that this is the debate you want, so they don't back off.
how_to_apply: Interrupt gently to affirm: 'This is good. Keep going.' Then let the debate run.
example_line: This is exactly the argument we need to have. Carry on.
markers: Affirmations during disagreement
Tom stepping in to smooth over early
common_mistakes: Letting conflict turn personal without intervening
drill: When the coach detects disagreement between others, it checks whether Tom affirmed or shut it down.

name: Restore mutual purpose
summary: When a conversation turns defensive, step out of the content and re-establish the goal you both share.
how_to_apply: Notice silence or attack; pause; state the shared goal; ask if they agree with it before returning to the issue.
example_line: Let me step back. We both want this client to renew. Can we start from there?
markers: Mutual-purpose statements after tension
Signs of silence (short answers) or attack (interruptions, raised loudness) before
common_mistakes: Stating a 'shared' goal that is really Tom's
Using it to dodge the issue
drill: In the next tense exchange, Tom names the shared goal before continuing; the coach checks the other person's next turn.

name: Contrast: what I don't mean and what I do
summary: Clarifying what you don't mean before saying what you do helps prevent the other person hearing an attack.
how_to_apply: When a message could be misread, say 'I'm not saying X; I am saying Y'.
example_line: I'm not saying the work is poor. I am saying it's not ready for the board yet.
markers: Contrasting statements ('I'm not saying... I am saying')
common_mistakes: Using it as a 'no offence, but' before an insult
drill: In each difficult feedback conversation, Tom uses one contrasting statement where misreading is likely.

name: Start with facts, offer the story tentatively
summary: Begin hard conversations with observable facts, share your interpretation as a possibility, and ask for theirs.
how_to_apply: Order: what I saw, what I'm starting to conclude, how do you see it? Use tentative wording on the conclusion.
example_line: You've missed the last two deadlines. I'm starting to wonder if the workload's too much. What's your view?
markers: Facts before judgements
Tentative markers on interpretations
Explicit request for their view
common_mistakes: So tentative the point is lost
Opening with the conclusion ('you're not committed')
drill: For the next difficult conversation, Tom plans facts, story and question in that order; the coach checks the order.

name: Ask for their story first
summary: Inviting the other person's account early, and listening fully, reduces defensiveness and often changes the picture.
how_to_apply: Ask an open question about how they see it and paraphrase back before responding.
example_line: How do you see what happened? ... So for you the brief changed late. Have I got that right?
markers: Open question + paraphrase before Tom's view
Tom interrupting the other person's account (`interruptions`)
common_mistakes: Paraphrasing as a technique without changing anything
drill: In each conflict conversation, Tom paraphrases the other's view and gets a 'yes' before giving his own.

name: Name the emotion, then the issue
summary: Acknowledging feelings plainly lowers the temperature and lets the conversation move to the issue.
how_to_apply: Reflect the emotion you hear in neutral words, pause, then return to the substance.
example_line: You sound pretty frustrated about the reorg. That's understandable. Let's talk about what we can change.
markers: Emotion labels
De-escalation in the other person's next turn (shorter, calmer)
common_mistakes: Telling people how they feel
Getting stuck on feelings and never reaching the issue
drill: Practise one emotion acknowledgement per difficult conversation; the coach checks the other person's next turn.

name: Allow pauses after hard news
summary: After delivering difficult news, leaving silence lets the other person respond rather than being talked over.
how_to_apply: Say the hard thing, then stop. Wait for them before adding explanation.
example_line: We're not going to put you forward this round. ... (pause)
markers: Gap after Tom's hard-news turn before he speaks again
Tom filling silence with justifications
common_mistakes: Long silences used to pressure
drill: After delivering bad news, Tom waits for the other person to speak first; the coach checks who broke the silence.

name: Side by side against the problem
summary: Frame the conflict as both people versus the problem, not versus each other.
how_to_apply: Use joint language ('how do we solve this?') and describe the problem as external and shared.
example_line: This isn't you versus me; it's both of us versus a deadline that doesn't work.
markers: 'We vs the problem' framing
'You always / you never' and character labels
common_mistakes: Pretending there's no real disagreement
drill: In the next disagreement, Tom reframes once as 'us versus the problem'.

name: Avoid 'you always', 'you never'
summary: Absolute words about people escalate conflict and invite counterexamples instead of change.
how_to_apply: Replace generalisations with a specific recent example and its effect.
example_line: Last Tuesday the update came after the deadline; that left Sara short.
markers: Absolutes about people ('always', 'never', 'every time')
common_mistakes: Over-correcting into vagueness
drill: The coach flags absolutes in Tom's conflict turns for a month.

name: Raise the elephant early
summary: Raise the difficult topic early in the conversation rather than leaving it to the last minutes or not at all.
how_to_apply: Plan the one hard point and say it in the first few minutes, after a brief opening.
example_line: There's something I want to raise today that's a bit awkward: the client complaint about your call.
markers: Time into the conversation before the difficult topic
Planned topic missing entirely
common_mistakes: Blurting it with no framing
Leaving it to the last two minutes
drill: Before each difficult conversation, Tom names the topic to the coach; the coach checks when it was raised.

name: Disagree upward respectfully
summary: Leaders also need to challenge decisions above them, clearly and with reasons, before committing.
how_to_apply: State the disagreement, reasons and what would change your mind; then commit if the decision stands.
example_line: I disagree, and here's why. If you still want to go ahead, I'll back it.
markers: Clear upward disagreement statements
Silence in upward meetings followed by complaints afterwards
common_mistakes: Disagreeing in private, complying in public then undermining
Repeated relitigation
drill: In the next meeting with a senior stakeholder where Tom disagrees, he states it with reasons in the meeting.

name: Move to action at the end
summary: Difficult conversations should end with who will do what, by when, and how follow-up happens; otherwise agreement evaporates.
how_to_apply: Summarise what you agreed, the actions and owners, and when you'll check in.
example_line: So you'll talk to the client, I'll adjust the scope, and we'll check in Friday.
markers: Action summary at the end of a conflict conversation
common_mistakes: Ending on relief with no plan
drill: Close every difficult conversation with an action summary; the coach checks the last minute.

name: Apologise when you've caused harm
summary: A brief, sincere apology for your own part restores safety faster than defending intent.
how_to_apply: Name what you did, its impact, and what you'll do differently; don't add 'but'.
example_line: I cut you off in front of the client. That wasn't fair, and I'll make sure it doesn't happen again.
markers: Specific apologies (`apologies` count with an act named)
'Sorry, but' patterns
common_mistakes: Reflexive 'sorry' that means nothing
Apologising for things that aren't Tom's
drill: When the coach detects a conflict that Tom contributed to, it checks for a specific apology in the next conversation with that person.

name: Name the meeting type and output
summary: Different meetings (decision, problem-solving, update, 1:1) need different structures; mixing them muddles both.
how_to_apply: At the start, say the type and the output ('this is a decision meeting; we leave with a yes or no on X') and who decides.
example_line: This is a decision meeting. By 11 we need a go or no-go on the pilot, and it's my call.
markers: Type + output + decider in the first two minutes
Update items crowding out decision items
common_mistakes: Stating an output that's never reached
Running every meeting as a status round
drill: For two weeks, Tom opens each meeting he chairs with type, output and decider; the coach checks the first two minutes.

name: Frame agenda items as questions
summary: Agenda items phrased as questions to answer focus discussion better than topic labels.
how_to_apply: Turn 'Pricing' into 'Should we raise prices in Q1, and by how much?' and read the question out at the start of the item.
example_line: Next item isn't 'pricing'; it's 'do we raise prices in January, yes or no?'
markers: Items introduced as questions vs topics
common_mistakes: Questions so broad they don't focus anything
drill: Tom rewrites his next three agendas as questions and reads each one out.

name: Keep tactical and strategic separate
summary: Weekly tactical meetings should handle near-term issues; big strategic topics deserve their own time rather than being squeezed in.
how_to_apply: When a strategic topic surfaces in a tactical meeting, park it explicitly to a dedicated session with a date and owner.
example_line: That's a big one; let's not do it in ten minutes. I'll set up an hour on it next Thursday.
markers: Parking statements with date and owner
Strategic debates squeezed into the last minutes
common_mistakes: Parking everything hard and never scheduling it
drill: The coach checks parked topics resurface in a later recording within a month.

name: Round-robin on key items
summary: Hearing briefly from everyone on important items brings out unshared information and reduces dominance by a few voices.
how_to_apply: Go round the room with a time limit ('30 seconds each'), starting with the most junior, before open discussion.
example_line: Quick round, 30 seconds each, starting with Jo: what's your read?
markers: Distinct speakers per item
Spread of `talk_share` across participants
Order: junior people first vs senior first
common_mistakes: Round-robins on trivial items
Letting it overrun
drill: In each team meeting, run at least one round-robin; the coach checks the number of distinct speakers on that item.

name: Invite the quiet expert by name
summary: Specific invitations to people with relevant knowledge, especially those who've not spoken, surface information that otherwise stays hidden.
how_to_apply: Name the person and ask a specific, answerable question tied to their expertise.
example_line: Amir, you ran the last migration. What's the risk we're missing?
markers: Named invitations
Speakers who contribute only after an invitation
Participants with zero turns
common_mistakes: Putting people on the spot with a vague question
Always inviting the same people
drill: The coach lists participants with no turns after each meeting; Tom invites at least one by name next time.

name: Keep the leader's airtime in check
summary: When the most senior person dominates airtime, others contribute less and the group's information pool shrinks; dominant talkers also overrate the meeting.
how_to_apply: Watch Tom's share of talk against the fair share for the meeting; shorten turns; end turns with a question.
example_line: That's my view in brief. Who sees it differently?
markers: Tom's `talk_share` vs fair share (1/participants)
`longest_turn_s` and `mean_turn_s`
Turns ending in a question
common_mistakes: Going silent in meetings where a clear lead is needed
drill: The coach reports Tom's talk share vs fair share after every team meeting; aim to be within 1.5 times fair share in discussion meetings.

name: Redirect complaint cycles to action
summary: In team meetings, complaining loops are linked to worse outcomes while solution and action talk goes with better ones.
how_to_apply: When problem-talk repeats, acknowledge it and ask 'what can we do about it this week?'.
example_line: We've named the problem three ways. What can we actually do about it by Friday?
markers: Ratio of solution/action talk to complaint talk
Redirection statements
Complaint chains (several complaint turns in a row)
common_mistakes: Shutting down legitimate concerns as 'negativity'
drill: The coach flags complaint chains of three or more turns; Tom practises redirecting within one turn of the flag.

name: Prioritise and execute under pressure
summary: When many problems hit at once, pick the most important one, focus the group on it, then move to the next.
how_to_apply: Say 'we can't solve all of these now; the one that matters most is X', and focus discussion there.
example_line: Five problems on the table. The one that matters this week is the client escalation. Everything else waits.
markers: Explicit prioritisation statements in crowded discussions
common_mistakes: Choosing by urgency over importance
drill: In the next overloaded meeting, Tom names the single most important issue before any discussion.

name: Summarise as you go
summary: Periodic short summaries keep the group aligned, show listening and make the decision point visible.
how_to_apply: Every 10-15 minutes, summarise where the group has got to and what's still open.
example_line: So far: we agree on scope, we disagree on timing. Let's spend ten minutes on timing.
markers: Summary statements mid-meeting
Discussions drifting without a summary
common_mistakes: Summaries that tilt the discussion to Tom's view
drill: The coach counts mid-meeting summaries; aim for one per major item.

name: Agree what we'll tell others
summary: Leadership teams should leave each meeting agreeing what to cascade to their teams, so messages are consistent.
how_to_apply: In the last minutes, ask: 'What are we each telling our teams, and what stays in the room?'
example_line: Before we go: what are we telling our teams, and by when?
markers: Cascade question in the close
Inconsistent messages reported later
common_mistakes: Skipping it because 'it's obvious'
drill: Add the cascade question to the close of every leadership meeting for a month.

name: Recap decisions, owners and dates
summary: End each meeting with a spoken recap of what was decided and who is doing what by when.
how_to_apply: Reserve the last three minutes; read back decisions and actions; ask 'what have I missed?'.
example_line: Recap: we launch in March; Dan owns pricing by Friday; I brief the CEO tomorrow. Anything missing?
markers: Decisions + owners + dates in the last three minutes
Meetings ending abruptly or overrunning with no recap
common_mistakes: Tom taking most actions himself
drill: The coach checks the last three minutes of each meeting for a recap with owners and dates.

name: Questions first on a pre-read
summary: When people have read a proposal beforehand (or in the first minutes), discussion can start from questions rather than a presentation.
how_to_apply: Circulate the paper, or give silent reading time, then open with 'questions and challenges' instead of presenting slides.
example_line: You've all read it, so no presentation. Who wants to start with the toughest question?
markers: Opening with questions vs Tom presenting
Long Tom monologues at the start (`longest_turn_s`)
common_mistakes: Pre-reads nobody reads
Silent reading on trivial topics
drill: For the next three proposal meetings, Tom does no presentation and opens with questions.

name: Same standing review each week
summary: Reviewing the same small set of measures and commitments in a fixed order makes problems visible early and accountability routine.
how_to_apply: Keep a fixed opening sequence (actions, three metrics, risks) each week, then new items.
example_line: Standard start: actions, then the three numbers, then risks.
markers: Standing items across recordings of the same meeting
common_mistakes: Ritual review that never changes decisions
drill: Fix the opening sequence for Tom's weekly team meeting and keep it for six weeks.

name: Frame the work as uncertain
summary: When the leader says openly that the work is new and uncertain, people see speaking up as part of the job rather than a risk.
how_to_apply: Open projects or discussions by naming what's unknown and why everyone's input is needed.
example_line: We've not done this before and I'll miss things. I need you to flag anything that looks off.
markers: Uncertainty framing at the start
Explicit requests for input
common_mistakes: Framing everything as uncertain so nothing feels decided
drill: Tom opens each project kick-off with one sentence on what's unknown and one asking for challenge.

name: Say 'I don't know' and 'I was wrong'
summary: Leaders who admit limits and mistakes make it safer for others to do the same, which supports team learning.
how_to_apply: When you don't know, say so and ask who does; when you got something wrong, say so plainly and move on.
example_line: I got that wrong last month. Here's what I've learned.
markers: Fallibility statements
Others admitting errors after Tom does
common_mistakes: Constant self-deprecation that erodes confidence, especially when competence is still being established
drill: Tom makes one genuine 'I don't know' or 'I was wrong' statement a week in team settings.

name: Model curiosity with genuine questions
summary: Asking genuine questions (ones you don't know the answer to) signals that others' knowledge matters.
how_to_apply: Ask questions that start from not knowing ('what are you seeing that I'm not?') rather than testing questions.
example_line: What are you seeing from the front line that I can't see from here?
markers: Genuine vs test questions
Others' answer length after Tom's questions
common_mistakes: Questions with an obvious 'right answer'
drill: In each meeting, Tom asks one question that starts with 'what am I missing?' or similar.

name: Thank the messenger
summary: How the leader reacts when someone raises a problem or mistake decides whether people will raise the next one.
how_to_apply: First response to bad news: thanks, then a forward-looking question. Hold frustration for later, if at all.
example_line: Thanks for flagging that early. What do we need to do in the next 24 hours?
markers: Tom's next turn after a problem disclosure: thanks/question vs blame/sarcasm
Whether the messenger speaks again later
Loudness or pitch spikes on that turn (EP coach owns delivery; leadership coach notes the content)
common_mistakes: Thanking then grilling
Shooting the messenger with a sigh or sarcasm
drill: The coach finds every bad-news moment and scores Tom's first response; aim for thanks + forward question every time.

name: Destigmatise failure
summary: Distinguish preventable errors, complex failures and intelligent experiments, and respond to each appropriately rather than punishing all failure.
how_to_apply: When something fails, ask which kind it was; celebrate intelligent failures and focus on learning, not blame.
example_line: This was a smart experiment that didn't work. What did we learn that's worth the cost?
markers: Failure classification language
Blame language after failures
common_mistakes: Celebrating sloppiness as 'failing fast'
drill: After each setback, Tom labels the failure type aloud before discussing it.

name: Ask directly for concerns
summary: Managerial openness (actively asking and responding) predicts whether people speak up more than general inspiring leadership does.
how_to_apply: Ask specific questions like 'what concerns you about this?' and 'what would you do differently?'; leave silence for answers.
example_line: What concerns you most about this plan? Even half-formed worries.
markers: Concern-seeking questions
Silence tolerated after the question
Concerns raised after invitations
common_mistakes: 'Any questions?' asked while closing the laptop
Inviting concerns and dismissing them
drill: End every proposal discussion with a specific concern question and a ten-second wait.

name: Close the loop on input
summary: People speak up again when they see their input acted on, or hear why it wasn't.
how_to_apply: Refer back to suggestions people made and say what happened to them.
example_line: Last month Jo suggested weekly client calls. We tried it; churn dropped. Thanks, Jo.
markers: References to earlier input and its outcome
common_mistakes: Pretending to have acted on everything
drill: Each month, Tom names two suggestions from his team in a meeting and what happened to them.

name: Avoid the accidental diminisher moves
summary: Well-meaning habits (always having ideas, rescuing, being always on, quick answers) can shrink others' contribution.
how_to_apply: Notice when Tom jumps in with ideas, rescues people or speaks after every turn; deliberately hold back.
example_line: I'm going to sit on my hands for this one. Over to you.
markers: Tom speaking after every other speaker (turn pattern)
Tom offering ideas in most turns
Rescue moves
common_mistakes: Overcorrecting into disengagement
drill: The coach reports the share of other speakers' turns immediately followed by Tom; aim to reduce it.

name: Report back on your own commitments
summary: Trust rests on ability, benevolence and integrity; keeping and reporting on your own promises is visible integrity.
how_to_apply: When you commit to something in a meeting, report back on it unprompted next time, including when you've missed it.
example_line: I said I'd get us the extra budget. I got half; here's why and what's next.
markers: Tom's own commitments from one recording reported in the next
Others reminding Tom of things he promised
common_mistakes: Over-promising to please
drill: The coach tracks Tom's spoken commitments and checks for an unprompted report-back in the next recording.

name: Explain changes of course
summary: When plans or decisions change, explaining what changed and why keeps credibility; silent reversals feel arbitrary.
how_to_apply: Name the change, the new information, and what it means for people.
example_line: We said Q1. We're moving to Q2 because the supplier slipped; here's what that means for you.
markers: Explicit explanations of changes
Reversals with no reason given
common_mistakes: Over-explaining small tweaks
drill: Each time Tom changes a prior decision, the coach checks for the what-changed-and-why pattern.

name: Show genuine care for the person
summary: Leaders who show care for people as people earn the trust that makes direct challenge possible.
how_to_apply: Ask about what matters to the person, remember it, and respond to life events with flexibility.
example_line: How did your daughter's first week at school go?
markers: Personal questions and remembered details
Purely transactional 1:1s
common_mistakes: Performative care
Intruding on privacy
drill: Tom follows up on one personal detail per 1:1 for a month.

name: Take the blame, give the credit
summary: Leaders who absorb blame outward and pass credit to the team build loyalty and safety.
how_to_apply: In front of seniors or clients, use 'I' for problems and name team members for successes.
example_line: The delay was my call. The fix was the team's, and Mo in particular.
markers: 'I' in failure talk to seniors; named credit for success
Blaming team members in front of others
common_mistakes: Absorbing blame for genuine performance issues that need addressing privately
drill: In each upward or client meeting, the coach checks pronouns in failure and success talk.

name: Match style to the moment
summary: Effective leaders shift among styles (visionary, coaching, affiliative, democratic, and occasionally directive) as situations demand; pacesetting and commanding styles hurt climate when overused.
how_to_apply: Name the moment: crisis needs direction, a new direction needs vision, a skilled team needs consultation. Notice when Tom defaults to setting the pace himself.
example_line: This is a crisis, so I'm going to be directive for 48 hours; then we'll debrief together.
markers: Proportion of directive vs consultative turns by setting
Pacesetting signals: Tom doing the work, impatience ('just do it like I would')
common_mistakes: Using the commanding style in non-crises
Taking published climate-to-results percentages as precise
drill: After each meeting, the coach labels Tom's dominant style and Tom checks whether it fit the situation.

name: Create urgency honestly
summary: Major change starts with enough people believing change is needed now; leaders build that by sharing real data and customer reality.
how_to_apply: Share unvarnished facts about the threat or opportunity and invite people to see it for themselves; don't invent a crisis.
example_line: Here are the last six months of churn by segment. Tell me if you see what I see.
markers: Evidence-based urgency statements
Others voicing the urgency themselves
common_mistakes: Manufactured 'burning platform' fear
Urgency without a path, which breeds anxiety
drill: In the next change discussion, Tom shares one piece of hard evidence and asks the team to draw the conclusion.
ethics_note: Exaggerating threat to create urgency is manipulative and erodes trust; urgency must rest on real facts.

name: Run decisions as conflicts of ideas, not people
summary: High-performing leadership teams argue hard about ideas, then align; the leader keeps the fight on the issue.
how_to_apply: Ask people to argue the other side's case first, then their own; stop personal remarks immediately.
example_line: Before you argue for your plan, give me the best version of Sam's.
markers: Steelman requests
Personal remarks in debate
common_mistakes: Debate that never ends in a decision
drill: In the next disagreement, Tom asks each side to state the other's case before arguing.

name: Level 5: ambition for the work, not yourself
summary: Collins described top leaders as combining personal humility with intense resolve for the organisation; the causal claim is disputed.
how_to_apply: In conversation, keep the focus on the organisation's results and others' contributions, and pair it with unwavering standards.
example_line: I don't care whose idea wins; I care that we hit the number.
markers: Self-reference vs organisation/team reference in success talk
Resolve statements on standards
common_mistakes: False modesty
Treating Level 5 as proven; the research design invites halo effects
drill: The coach tracks 'I' vs 'we/they' in Tom's success talk for a month.

name: Lead by asking, not telling (coach mindset)
summary: Great managers act as coaches: they ask, listen and help people find answers, rather than direct every move.
how_to_apply: In 1:1s and problem-solving moments, use a question first and offer direction only when needed.
example_line: What's your plan, and where would you like a second opinion?
markers: Ask:tell ratio
Report's share of solution ideas
common_mistakes: Coaching when a quick answer is needed
drill: The coach reports ask:tell for each 1:1; Tom aims for more questions than statements.

name: Tell one concrete story
summary: A single specific example, especially about a customer or colleague, often moves people more than abstract data alone.
how_to_apply: Pair the key number with one real, short story that shows what it means.
example_line: Churn's at 12 percent. Last week that was Acme, who'd been with us six years, leaving over one bad renewal call.
markers: Concrete examples with named people or customers alongside data
common_mistakes: Anecdote replacing evidence
Stories that are long or self-congratulatory
drill: For the next persuasive pitch, Tom pairs his main statistic with one 30-second story.
